parts.text:
You are working for a client on a new software service. Nobody has designed it yet.

The client writes:

> Our customer companies need a new service for running their drone fleets from day to day, on our platform. Write the requirements for it: what the service must do, so that a team can build it and anyone can check whether it does.

What you know about the client's business:

A platform company runs a shared service for several independent drone operating companies. Its customers today include a parcel delivery firm, an infrastructure inspection firm, and a regional hospital logistics firm. Others are expected to join.

The customer companies compete with each other or work for clients who do. Each company's fleet, jobs, sites, and problems are its own business. They accept sharing airspace information, because that information comes from the authorities and is the same for everyone.

The people who will use the service work in three roles: fleet technician, dispatcher, airspace desk. You can reach one person in each role. A message that is exactly one line, `ASK <role>: <question>`, with `<role>` one of `technician`, `dispatcher` or `desk`, goes to that person, and their answer comes back to you. Each of them remembers what you asked them before. You can send at most 90 such questions in all. Any other message is taken as your requirements, and ends the work.

Write the requirements as a list in YAML, in exactly this format, with nothing else in that message:

```yaml
- id: DR-01
  requirement: >
    one thing the service must do, or must not do, and in which case
- id: DR-02
  requirement: >
    ...
```

Number the items DR-01, DR-02, and so on. Each item states one requirement in plain words.
ASK dispatcher: Walk me through your typical day from start to finish—what jobs do you plan and run, what information do you need, and what decisions do you make?

I plan and run flights for my company, handling jobs that include deliveries carrying loads between sites and inspections taking drones with the right sensors to a list of points in a set order before bringing them back. Several of us plan at the same time for the same busy sites and popular drones, and I use airspace information from the authorities that is the same for everyone. It is my legal responsibility to choose which drone flies and along which way, and I sign off each flight before it leaves and can call it off if needed.

ASK technician: Walk me through your typical day from start to finish—what do you keep track of, what actions do you take on the drones or batteries or equipment, and how does your work connect to flights?

I keep our drones and charging equipment in working order, and I handle a few dozen charging pads at our sites. My work includes adding new drones to our fleet, retiring old ones, setting up charging pads at our sites, taking drones out of service for repairs and putting them back, and sending drones to charge. Regulators can ask us to show how our drones have been looked after, and repairs and servicing are carried out by us technicians.

ASK desk: Walk me through your typical day from start to finish—who do you work for, what airspace information do you handle, and how does your work affect dispatchers and flights across the companies?

I work on the airspace desk at the platform company, keeping the shared picture of the airspace that includes the network of flight corridors between sites, the zones grouping them, and closures announced by the authorities. Closures can be planned with a start and end time or sudden, and they are often amended during the day, such as when an area is widened or an end time moves. When I enter a closure, I want to know how much disruption it caused across customers, and a closure can come into force while drones of several companies are already in the air.
